phaseDescription.menstrual: Hormones are at their lowest, so cramps and tiredness are common. Keep your belly warm and rest a little more.
phaseDescription.follicular: Estrogen (the main female sex hormone) is rising and energy usually follows. A good stretch for exercise or getting things done.
phaseDescription.ovulation: LH (the hormone that signals the ovary to release an egg) surges, so you might feel a brief twinge on one side. This is also your most fertile day.
phaseDescription.luteal: Progesterone (the hormone that keeps the uterine lining thick) is rising, which can bring tender breasts or a shorter temper. Be gentle with yourself.

menstrual.food: Eat warm meals with iron (lean meat, beans, leafy greens) and drink enough water.
menstrual.move: Move gently if you feel up to it, rest if the cramps are bad.
menstrual.mind: Drop what isn't essential and rest when tired.
menstrual.sleep: A warm compress on your belly can help you sleep if it hurts.

follicular.food: Eat regular meals with enough protein and vegetables, and drink enough water.
follicular.move: Energy is rising, so you can train harder than usual.
follicular.mind: A good time to start things that need focus.
follicular.sleep: Keep a steady bedtime to hold on to your energy.

ovulation.food: Eat plenty of vegetables and fibre, and drink enough water.
ovulation.move: Exercise as usual, and warm up well.
ovulation.mind: Mood is often good. A slight twinge on one side is usually nothing to worry about.
ovulation.sleep: Keep the room cool to sleep more easily.

luteal.food: Cut back on salt and caffeine to ease bloating and tenderness.
luteal.move: Exercise at an easy pace and cut back if you feel tired.
luteal.mind: Feeling irritable or sensitive is common, so leave some time for yourself.
luteal.sleep: Go to bed a little earlier, your body needs more rest.

learn.title: Understanding your cycle
learn.intro: The menstrual cycle is the body's repeating monthly process that prepares for a possible pregnancy. A cycle runs from the first day of bleeding to the first day of the next period.

howCounted.title: How long is normal?
howCounted.body: Most cycles last 24 to 38 days, averaging around 28.

phase.menstrual: The egg from last cycle wasn't fertilized, so the uterine lining breaks down and sheds — this is your period, usually lasting 3 to 7 days. These are relatively safe days, but not completely safe, especially with short or irregular cycles.
phase.follicular: Starting alongside your period, the pituitary gland (a small gland at the base of the brain) prompts your ovaries to grow follicles (tiny sacs, each holding an immature egg) while rising estrogen (the main female sex hormone) thickens the uterine lining again. The first days are relatively safe, but the closer to ovulation the more dangerous they get, because sperm can survive in the body for up to about 5 days.
phase.ovulation: Around the middle of the cycle (day 14 in a 28-day cycle), a surge of LH (luteinizing hormone, the signal that triggers ovulation) causes a mature follicle to burst and release an egg. These are the most dangerous days: ovulation day and roughly the 5 days before it. If you're not trying to conceive, you need protection throughout this whole stretch.
phase.luteal: After ovulation, the burst follicle becomes the corpus luteum (a small temporary structure in the ovary) and releases progesterone (a hormone that keeps the lining thick) so the lining stays thick. Without fertilization, it breaks down, hormones drop, and the next period begins. About a day after ovulation these are relatively safe days. Calendar estimates of ovulation can be off, though, so don't rely on this as dependable contraception.

doctor.title: When to see a doctor
doctor.intro: Check in with a doctor if you notice:
doctor.item1: A cycle shorter than 24 days or longer than 38 days
doctor.item2: No period for 3 months or more
doctor.item3: Bleeding that lasts more than 8 days, or unusually heavy flow
doctor.item4: Severe pain with nausea during your period

lh.title: What is LH?
lh.body: LH (luteinizing hormone) is made by the pituitary gland, a small gland at the base of the brain. About a day before an egg is released, LH surges, which signals the ovary to release it. An LH test (ovulation strip) measures it in urine: a dark line (positive) means ovulation is probably very close, within 12 to 36 hours.

bbt.title: What is basal body temperature (BBT)?
bbt.body: BBT is your body temperature at full rest, taken right after waking, before you sit up or eat or drink. After ovulation, progesterone raises it slightly, about 0.2 to 0.5°C, and it stays up until the next period, so the chart can show whether ovulation has happened. Measure at the same time every morning with a thermometer accurate to 0.01°C.

cervicalMucus.title: What is cervical mucus?
cervicalMucus.body: A fluid made by the cervix that changes through the cycle. It is dry or scant after your period, then creamy. Near ovulation it turns clear, slippery and stretchy like raw egg white, the most fertile sign, because it helps sperm travel. After ovulation it turns thick and sticky again.

corpusLuteum.title: What is the corpus luteum?
corpusLuteum.body: After the egg is released, the empty follicle turns into the corpus luteum, a small temporary structure in the ovary. It makes progesterone for about 14 days. Without a pregnancy it breaks down and the next period starts. This stretch is called the luteal phase.

fertileWindow.title: What is the fertile window?
fertileWindow.body: The days when sex can lead to pregnancy: ovulation day and about 5 days before it, since sperm can live up to 5 days. It is a calendar estimate and can be off by a few days, so don't rely on it as contraception.

variation.title: What is cycle variation?
variation.body: How much your cycle lengths differ from one another. For example ±2 days means cycles are usually about 2 days longer or shorter than your average. The smaller it is, the more regular your cycle and the more accurate the prediction. (Mathematically it is the weighted standard deviation.)

weightedAverage.title: What is a weighted average?
weightedAverage.body: An average cycle length where recent cycles count more than old ones, because bodies change over time. Each cycle further back counts for 80% of the one after it. That multiplier is the weight.

confidence.title: What is confidence?
confidence.body: How sure Blushme is about your next period prediction. The more cycles you log and the more regular they are, the higher it gets. New users stay at low confidence until at least 3 cycles are logged.
